Immunology of Pregnancy

Maternal-fetal tolerance, implantation immunology, IDO1, inflammatory stages of pregnancy, hemolytic disease of the newborn, and infectious complications.

Semi-AllograftTregsIDO1Th1 ↔ Th2Rh Disease
Image rule
Only cropped lecture diagrams are embedded. The immune-mechanism explanation stays in the companion text rather than inside slide screenshots.

Learning objectives

A3.1. Explain how the embryo/fetus, as a semi-allograft, is protected from maternal immune attack.
A3.2. Compare blastocyst implantation with tumor immunology and transplant immunology.
A3.3. Explain the multiple reinforcing pathways that establish and maintain tolerance.
A3.4. Explain IDO1 in implantation and the consequence of IDO1 inhibition.
A3.5. Describe the beneficial and harmful roles of inflammation across the three immunologic stages of pregnancy; explain hemolytic disease of the newborn.
A3.6. Identify common infectious complications of pregnancy.

1. Why does the fetus not get rejected?

Core problem: the embryo/fetus expresses maternal + paternal antigens, making it a semi-allograft. The maternal immune system must tolerate fetal/paternal antigens without becoming globally immunosuppressed.

Potential danger signals

The lecture names MHC, minor transplantation antigens, and blood-group antigens as fetal foreign antigens that could theoretically trigger maternal immunity.

Not global immunosuppression

Pregnancy alters many innate and adaptive immune functions, but the mother must still maintain antimicrobial defense and tumor immunosurveillance.

Lecture framing
The lecture says this relationship has important features that are more like tumor immunology than classic transplant immunology: local invasion, tissue remodeling, and active mechanisms that blunt destructive immune responses without shutting down the entire immune system.

2. The three immunologic stages of pregnancy

Pattern to memorize: pro-inflammatory → anti-inflammatory → pro-inflammatory.
StageImmune milieuWhy it is useful
Implantation / placentationTh1-type, pro-inflammatoryTissue injury/repair, trophoblast implantation and placental formation
Fetal growthTh2-type, anti-inflammatoryMaternal-fetal tolerance and relatively homeostatic growth environment
Labor/deliverySecond pro-inflammatory stateHelps initiate labor and delivery
Cropped lecture diagram: implantation begins in a pro-inflammatory environment, with M1-type signals and trophoblast/decidual immune cross-talk.
Cropped lecture diagram: the fetal-growth phase shifts toward anti-inflammatory tolerance with M2-like macrophages, Tregs, Th2 cells, and cytokines such as IL-10/TGF-β.

Hormonal immunomodulation

HormoneImmune role emphasized in lecture
ProgesteronePrepares uterus for implantation; promotes expansion and function of regulatory T cells
EstradiolEncourages the shift from Th1 pro-inflammatory toward Th2 anti-inflammatory responses
hCGStimulates progesterone, facilitates trophoblast invasion, and contributes to immune modulation
Active-learning trap
The lecture's Th1 → Th2 shift question points to estradiol as the direct hormone encouraging that immune shift.

3. Implantation: apposition → adhesion → invasion

Implantation sequence: apposition → adhesion → invasion. The inflammatory response is not accidental; the lecture frames it as a controlled tissue-injury-and-repair process.
Cropped lecture diagram: trophoblast, stromal cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, NK cells, T cells, and spiral arteries participate in local implantation cross-talk.
StepLecture details
AppositionTrophoblast contacts the endometrial implantation site; vascular permeability increases under prostaglandins and cytokines, especially IL-1 and IL-6
AdhesionBlastocyst attaches to uterine epithelium; integrins, cadherins, and selectins facilitate attachment and decidual restructuring
InvasionEndometrial stromal and immune cells create an inflammatory environment with IL-6, IL-8, IL-15, GM-CSF, TNF, TGF-β, chemokines, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes
Tumor-immunology comparison
The lecture specifically compares trophoblast invasion with malignant-cell invasion because both breach tissue barriers and depend on local remodeling and immune modulation.

4. Maternal-fetal tolerance uses multiple reinforcing pathways

No single mechanism protects pregnancy. The lecture explicitly names cytokines, Tregs, HLA-G, and IDO1 as cooperating pathways.

Tregs

Regulatory T cells that recognize paternal antigens protect fetal cells from maternal immune attack.

Decidual macrophages

M2-like macrophages support tissue renewal, anti-inflammatory cytokine production, and removal of dying trophoblast cells before paternal antigens become inflammatory danger signals.

Decidual NK cells

The lecture presents NK cells as a major placental immune population participating in a specialized local tolerance/remodeling environment.

Placental immune-cell proportions

Lecture table: approximately 70% NK cells, 20% macrophages, 10% T cells, with few dendritic cells/B cells.

Autoimmune-disease pattern in lecture
During the Th2-dominant growth phase, Th1-mediated diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis may improve, while Th2-mediated disease such as neuromyelitis optica may worsen.

5. IDO1: the tolerance mechanism to know cold

IDO1 oxidizes L-tryptophan. The lecture says it is necessary for trophoblast invasion and maternal tolerance; IDO inhibition terminates pregnancy.

Metabolic effect

IDO1 catalyzes L-tryptophan oxidation.

Immune effect

Oxidized tryptophan metabolites are immunosuppressive, reducing cytotoxic T-cell responses and favoring Treg differentiation/activation.

Th17 connection

The lecture notes that IDO-associated pathways block conversion toward Th17-like cells.

Clinical parallel

Tumors can exploit IDO-mediated immune evasion; therefore IDO inhibitors are being explored to enhance anti-tumor immunity.

Exam-level prediction
If a pregnant patient receives an effective IDO inhibitor in early pregnancy, the lecture's predicted consequence is termination of pregnancy.

6. Hemolytic disease of the newborn

Cropped lecture diagram: RhD-negative mother becomes sensitized to an RhD-positive fetus; anti-RhD IgG can threaten a later RhD-positive pregnancy.
Mechanism: maternal anti-RhD IgG crosses the placenta and destroys RhD-positive fetal RBCs.
PointLecture emphasis
At-risk pairingRhD-negative mother + RhD-positive father / fetus
First pregnancyUsually sensitization rather than severe fetal disease
Later RhD+ pregnancyHigh-titer maternal anti-RhD IgG crosses placenta and attacks fetal RBCs
Other antigen systemsAB, MNS, Kidd, Duffy; Kell can produce neonatal anemia by other mechanisms
PreventionLecture case resolution: anti-RhD immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) prevents maternal sensitization
IgG transport cuts both ways
FcRn actively transfers maternal IgG across the placenta. That gives the newborn passive immunity, but there is no mechanism that selectively blocks maternal pathogenic IgG.
Other harmful maternal IgG examples from lecture
Neonatal lupus (anti-Ro/SSA and/or La/SSB), neonatal pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, and immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

7. Infectious complications of pregnancy

TORCH

Lecture TORCH list: Toxoplasma • Rubella • Cytomegalovirus • Herpes simplex.

Three ways pregnancy changes infectious risk

CategoryExamples listed in lecture
Increased maternal susceptibilityListeriosis; tuberculosis in the puerperium; malaria
Increased maternal severityInvasive H. influenzae, pneumococcal disease, invasive GAS, influenza, VZV, primary HSV, measles, hepatitis E, malaria, dengue/Lassa/Ebola, coccidioidomycosis
Severe fetal outcomesToxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV, HSV, HBV, HIV, syphilis, parvovirus B19, primary VZV, influenza, GBS, plus malaria/listeriosis/TB/Zika/measles/mumps
Important framing
Pregnancy is not generalized immunosuppression. Infection patterns reflect physiologic, endocrine, and immunologic changes while immune protection remains active.
